sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: Why not? Doesn’t she want him?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: It doesn’t seem likely, does it? He’s not exactly a tender morsel for her young teeth.

sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: No, you can’t blame her, can you? What does she say?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Nothing at all. How could she, when I’ve not been able to see her? When I got there and asked for her, those jaileresses at the convent just tried to take the mickey out of me.

sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: It wasn’t your mickey they were after, it was your dickey. You don’t know what they’re like.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: I know them better than you do, pox rot ’em! You should have seen them. One asks me if I fancy her, if I’d be prepared to marry her. Another says Lelia’s just out of the tub in the dormitory, being dried; so someone else says she’s being pressed in the cloister. And then another asks (imitating) ‘Did your father have any male children?’ So I nearly told them to f... find out for themselves. But in the end I saw they were teasing me to put me off, they didn’t want me to talk to Lelia.

sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: You missed your chance. You should have thrust your way in, and said you’d look for her yourself.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Poxing hell! Go in there alone? What do you take me for? A randy stud stallion couldn’t do their business for them without help. Nuns! I ask you. But I can’t stand here talking to you, I’ve got to report to my boss.

sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: And I’ve got to go and buy civet for mine — the lunatic!

div2.head: Scene 1
div2.stage: LELIA as ‘Fabio’; FLAMMINIO, a young man in love

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: It really makes no sense to me, Fabio! After all this while, you have still not been able to obtain any response from this cruel, ungracious Isabella. And yet, if she is always prepared to listen to you, and if she welcomes you so eagerly, it is hard to believe that she actually dislikes me: after all, I have never done anything which could displease her, as far as I know. You would be able to gather, wouldn’t you, from her conversation, if she had any cause to see me as her enemy? Tell me again, Fabio, please: just what did she say last night when you went there with that letter?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I’ve told you a dozen times over already, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: So tell me again. What concern is it of yours?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What concern? I’m concerned, sir, because I can see that it makes you unhappy, and that hurts me as much as it does you. Being your servant, I am supposed to try to please you at all times — and listening to these answers of hers, you might end by blaming me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Don’t be afraid of that, Fabio my boy — I’m as fond of you as I am of my own brother. I know how loyal you are to me, and you can count on my standing by you always. You’ll see what I mean, in time, if you can wait just a while. But what did she say?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What I told you before: that the greatest favour in the world that you can do her is to leave her in peace and forget about her, because her thoughts are turned elsewhere; that she is not sufficiently her own mistress even to be able to look at you, because her eyes are slaves to another; that you are wasting your time and energy in pursuing her, because you will be left at the end clutching nothing but the empty air.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: But do you think, Fabio, that she really means these things she says, or is it just that she’s offended with something I’ve done? Because there was a time when she seemed quite amiable towards me, and I can hardly believe that she dislikes me when she keeps accepting my letters and messages. I shall continue to plead with her, come what may. Sooner or later she will succumb. What do you say, Fabio? Don’t you think so?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I think not, my lord.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: But why?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Because if I were in your place, I should at the very least expect to be allowed to see her. It’s not as though a man like you can be short of interested ladies — you’re well born, high-minded, dignified, handsome.... Take my advice, master: let her alone, and devote yourself to someone else who loves you. You’ll find such a one, you’ll see, and probably just as pretty as Isabella. Think now, is there no one in this town who would be glad if you were to love her?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: More than a few, of course! There’s one in particular among all the others, called Lelia — do you know, you look amazingly like her, I’ve been meaning to say so several times. She’s reckoned to be the prettiest, the shrewdest, the most spirited girl in town. I must point her out to you one day. She would be overjoyed if I paid her some attention: she’s rich, she’s been in court, and she was my sweetheart for nearly a year. She made it clear scores of times how she felt, and then all of a sudden she went off to Mirandola. And my evil luck made me fall in love with Isabella, who has been as cold towards me as Lelia was kind.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Master, in that case you deserve whatever sufferings you get, because if you have someone who loves you, and you don’t appreciate her, it’s only justice that another woman should not appreciate you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: If that poor young lady was in love with you before, and still loves you more than ever, why did you cast her aside to follow someone else? I don’t know if God can ever forgive such a sin. My lord Flamminio, you are doing a great wrong.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You’re still only a boy, Fabio, you don’t understand the strength of love. I say that I am compelled to love this Isabella; I dote on her; I cannot and I will not think of anyone but her. So you must go back and talk to her, and see if you can tease out of her just what it is that I’ve done that makes her refuse even to see me.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: You are wasting your time, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: My time is my own to waste.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: It will be no use.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: So be it.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Let her go, sir — I’m sure I’m right.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I cannot. Go along now, if you please.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Very well then, but....

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Come back straight away with her answer. I’m going as far as the Cathedral.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: At the first suitable moment I’ll approach her.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Fabio, if you succeed in this, you can name your own reward.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: He’s away just in time. Here’s Pasquella on her way to find me.

div2.head: Scene 2
div2.stage: PASQUELLA, servant to Gherardo; LELIA as Fabio

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (to audience) I don’t think there’s anything more troublesome in the world, for someone like me, than to be in the service of a young woman in love. And it’s even worse with one like my mistress, who doesn’t have to worry about a mother, or sisters, or anyone else who might find out. The last few days she's been getting so itchy and so frantic, there’s no peace by night or by day. She keeps scratching away at her... pincushion, kneading at her thighs, one minute she dashes to the window, then downstairs, then up again; she won’t stand still for a minute, you’d think she had quicksilver on her feet. Lord save us! I don’t know, I’ve had my share of being young and in love, and I’ve done some things in my time; but I did use to sit down occasionally. It wouldn’t be so bad if she’d latched on to a man of some substance and experience, who knew what he was up to and could scratch her itch for her properly! But she’s gone all soft over a silly little boy who’s hardly got the sense to do up his own breeches without some help. And she keeps sending me out after this handsome swain at all hours of the day, as though I hadn’t enough to keep me busy in the house. And while all this is going on, his boss still thinks that he’s just acting as a go-between. But there he is, coming this way. That’s a piece of luck! Fabio, a very good day to you. I was on my way to find you, my sweetheart.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: And a thousand ducats to you, Pasquella my love. And what is your beautiful mistress up to? What did she want me for?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What do you think she’s doing? She’s weeping, she’s wilting, she’s wasting away, because you haven’t paid her a call yet this morning.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Does she expect me to turn up before it’s even light?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I think she’d like it even better if you stayed with her all night.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Not likely! I’ve got other things to do. I’ve got to wait on my master, haven’t I?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh, I’m sure your master wouldn’t miss you if you came here. After all, you don’t sleep with him — or do you?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I wish to Heaven I were that much in his favour! Then I wouldn’t be in the trouble I’m in now.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Come on, now! Wouldn’t you rather sleep with Isabella?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Not I.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Hey! You’re having me on.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I wish I were.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well, anyway.... My mistress begs you to come to her straight away, because her father has gone out and she wants to talk to you about something important.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Tell her that if she doesn’t get rid of Flamminio, she’s wasting her time: she knows quite well that it would be all up with me if I were found cheating my master.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Come and tell her yourself.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I tell you I’m busy. Didn’t you hear?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Busy with what? Go on, pop in for a moment: you don’t have to stay long.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Stop pestering me, for goodness sake. Take yourself off.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You won’t come, then?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: No, I’ve told you. How many more times?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well really, I must say, young Fabio, you think a great deal of yourself. If you want my opinion, you’re just a silly child who doesn’t know when he’s well off. You’re not always going to be mooned over like this, you know. Those whiskers will come, sooner or later; and then you won’t have your tender pink cheeks and your little rosebud lips, and there won’t be quite so many people chasing after you, will there? The you’ll realize what a fool you were, and you’ll be sorry when it’s too late. How many men do you think there are in this town who would give anything for Isabella just to throw a glance in their direction? And all you can do is turn your nose up — talk about pearls before swine!

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Why doesn’t she throw them a few glances, then? Perhaps she’d leave me in peace.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Good God! I know young men are not supposed to have much sense, but....

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Come on now, Pasquella! Stop preaching at me, you’re only making things worse.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You supercilious little urchin, you'll be sorry when you get off your high horse! (Changing tone) Oh come on now, Fabio my love, my honeybunch! Come and see her, do me a favour; otherwise she’ll only send me out after you again, she won’t even believe I found you the first time.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: All right! Go along now, Pasquella, I’ll come. I was only teasing you.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: When, my sweetheart?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Soon.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: How soon?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Right away. Go on, now.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’ll be waiting for you on the doorstep.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Yes, yes, all right!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Hey! Do you hear me? If you don’t come soon, I’ll give you what for!

div2.head: Scene 3

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Por mi vida! Hhere I see before me ze anthient and fortunate vooman hhose mistress is ze hhandsomest señorita in all zis thitty thitty Lilias’s pronunciation: A double ‘h’ is used to represent a guttural ‘ch’ sound, as in Scottish ‘loch’ or the first sound of Spanish junta, gente . An accent on a vowel indicates a stressed syllable; and a dieresis over an ‘e’ (‘possethiónës’) shows that it is pronounced as a separate syllable. . If only I could make ze occasión to strike up a conversathión viz hher, in secret and vizout testimonies! I svear by ze chastity of all ze hholy priests in Rome zat I vould make hher sqveal like a cat in ze hhayloft! I shall try my blandishments upon hher, and dethieve zis shoddy and corrupt old hhag into giving me all her possethiónës. Buenos días , señora Pasquella, flower of hhentility! Hhwere hhave you been at zis premature hour of ze day?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh! Good day to you Señor Lilias! And where are you on your way to?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I go hhunting for adventura , zat I might find some vooman to bestow hher caresses upon me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (ironic) Of course! You Spaniards can’t get rid of them, can you? Not a single one of you that hasn’t got a dozen of us poor females just waiting on his pleasure!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: To speak truth, I hhave but two, dos — but I cannot visit eizer vun vizout periglo extremo , extreme peril!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh really? They’ll be gentlewomen, no doubt, from the best known ‘houses’.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Exactamente. But I am now in search of a matron hhoo might launder my shirts for me, repair my breeches and doublet, and treat me as hher own son — and I in my turn vould serve hher viz devothión.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well, keep on searching, you're bound to find someone eventually. A man who traffics with gentlewomen should have no trouble with servants.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: She is already found, viz your permithión.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Who is she?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Yourselve.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What? I’m too old for you.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Old? I svear by ze Virgen María of Monserrato zat I took you for an infanta of fifteen or tventy yearss! Por favor , do not speak of yourselve so, it cautheth me much pain. Consider razzer if you may do me some favor , and zen you vill see if I treat you as old or as young.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh no, none of your swaggering. I’m having no truck with Spaniards. You’re like hornets, you lot: even if you don’t sting, you pester the life out of people. Dealing with you is like picking up coal: you either burn your hand or get it dirty. No good comes of mixing in your affairs.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: No good? Madre de Diós , you vill benefit more from me zan from ze greatest nobleman of zis town. Perhhaps I may seem in some small poverty at zis moment, but I am vun of ze best and most hhighly born hidalgos of Spain.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (to audience) It’s a wonder he didn’t say ‘Duke’ or ‘Knight’ — all the Spaniards that come over here make out they’re lords of some kind. And look at them!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Pasquella, acthept my protecthión, and you vill gain great things.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Why, what will you give me, for heaven’s sake?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I vish nothing but zat you should be my muzzer, mi madre . And I vill be your liddle son, and sometimes your hhusband too if you vish.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Hey, leave me alone! Not likely!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (to audience) She laughéd! Victory! She vill yield to my persuathiónës!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What did you say?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I vish to give you a rosary for your devothiónës.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Where is it then?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Behhold.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh, but that’s a necklace! (He snatches it away.) I thought you wanted to give it to me.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: If you vill consent to be my muzzer, please, zen I give it to you.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’ll be anything you like if I can have it.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwen may ve hhave a liddle conversathión togezzer — chust a short time?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Whenever you like.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwere?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh... I don’t know where.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhave you not in your hhouze un lugar segreto , a secret place hhwere I may insert myselve zis evening?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well, there is somewhere... but suppose my master found out?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But no, hhe vill know nothing.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Listen, I’ll see if there’s any way of managing it this evening. You stroll by in front of the house, and I’ll let you know if you can come or not. Give me the necklace now, it’s a real beauty!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (holding on to it) Muy bien! I shall be ready and vaiting at dusk.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Yes, yes, of course, but let’s have the beads.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I shall bring zem viz me hhwen I come to your hhouze; before giving zem I vish to perfume zem a liddle.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh, I’m not fussy about that. I’ll take them as they are, I don’t want them scented.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But look, zis bead is broken. I must make it repairéd viz gold, and I give it to you zis evening. Is it not enough zat it vill be yourss?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It’ll be mine when I’ve got my hands on it, and not before. That’s what comes of believing what a Spaniard says to you. It’s just like I said: getting something out of you lot is like blood out of a stone.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But madre , my muzzer, hhwat are you saying?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’m going home, my mistress is waiting.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: No, vait a liddle! Hhwy so much hhurry? Hhwat business hhave you viz your mistress?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What do you think? Young women these days fall in love before you’ve stopped blowing their noses for them. If they’re not careful, before they start learning to sew, they’ll get ‘pricked’.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Qué queréis dezir ?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What’s that? ‘Rests here?’ No, she doesn’t rest here or anywhere, with the fidgets she’s got on her.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But tell me, por favor , viz hhoom is she in love? It seems not posible, she is too young.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It’s only too true. I wish it wasn’t, or I wish she’d picked on someone of her own station.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But tell me, I beg you: hhoo is hhe?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I shouldn’t talk about it, really. Well, make sure you don’t spread it around. You know that page boy who waits on Flamminio de’ Carandini?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat? Zat liddle boy hhoo is dressëd all in hhwite?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: That’s the one.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Váleme Diós! Is it posible ? Hhwat can she expect from him? Hhe seems vun to rethieve attenthiónës, not to give zem.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You can say that again.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: And zis liddle boy, hhe loves hher also?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It’s hard to say.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: But su padre , her fazzer, does hhe know of zis conspirathy?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Not as far as I can see. In fact he’s found the boy twice in his house now, and he’s made a great fuss of him — taken his hand, chucked him under the chin, as though the lad were his own son. He says he looks very like the daughter of Virginio Bellenzini.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Ah, ze filthy pig, perverted old svine! Sí, sí , it is clear hhwat hhe is vanting.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Hey, you’ve kept me here too long, I’ve got to go.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Listen: I vill come tonight. Do not forget your promise.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: And you don’t forget to bring the necklace.

div2.stage: (Both exit, Pasquella to Gherardo’s house, Lilias to town.)

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: FLAMMINIO; SIFTER, his servant; STOKE, servant to Virginio.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You still haven’t been to look for Fabio, as I told you, and he hasn’t come back yet. He’s been so long, I don’t know what to make of it.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I was just going, and you called me back for something else. It’s not my fault.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Go now, then. If you find that he’s still in with Isabella, wait until he comes out and then bring him straight back here.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: How am I supposed to know if he’s inside her house or not? Do you want me to ask for him at the door?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You stupid half-wit! Do you want to give me away? Good God, I haven’t a servant in the house who’s worth his keep, apart from Fabio. I only hope I can give him the reward he deserves. What do you say? What are you mumbling, you moron? Isn’t it true?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: What am I supposed to be saying? I’m agreeing with you, aren’t I? Fabio is honest, Fabio is pretty, Fabio is a good servant. Fabio in with you, Fabio in with my lady.... Fabio goes everywhere, Fabio does everything. Only....

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Only what?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: (muttering) He won’t always be such a pretty piece of goods.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What’s that about ‘goods’?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I say you shouldn’t trust him all the time with your goods. He’s only a foreigner, after all. One of these days he could diddle you and disappear with the lot.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I wish I could trust the rest of you as much! Look, there’s Stoke; go and ask him if he’s seen the boy. I shall be at the Porrini Exchange.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Hey, Stoke! Have you seen Fabio?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Who? That pretty boy of yours? You dirty dog, you’re on to a good thing there, aren’t you?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Where are you off to?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Looking for my old gaffer.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: He just went by not long ago.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Which way was he pointing?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Up that way. Come on, we'll find him together. Come on! I’ve got something to tell you about, a really juicy story that happened when I was in with Caterina. You’ll really crease yourself....

sp.speaker: PLUCK
sp.p: There’s nothing worse than having to run errands for a boss who’s off his rocker. Gherardo sends me to buy him that civet. When I asked at the perfume shop for it, and said I only had one bolognino to pay for it, he started saying that I must have remembered it all wrong, and that Gherardo must have wanted some itch ointment — ’cause he needs plenty of that, he said, and he’s never bought civet before. So to make him believe me, I started telling him about this love affair; and he nearly died laughing, along with some young fellows that were there, and wanted me to buy him a flask of bromide. So I came away with nothing, and looking a fool into the bargain. If the boss really wants some, then next time he’ll have to cough up a bit more.

div2.head: Scene 6
div2.stage: SIFTER; STOKE; then LELIA as a boy, and ISABELLA
(Sifter and Stoke emerge with howls of laughter)

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: There you are, what did I tell you? And if you want to come with me next time, I’ll find you another one just like her.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Get to work on it then: because if you can find me a girl who takes my fancy, I swear I’ll lay on a really good time for the two of us. I’ve got the keys to the granary, the cellar, the larder, and the wood store: all I need is a good bunk-up when I feel like it, and I reckon you and me could live in clover. After all, it’s the only way to get anything out of working for these bosses.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Well, I’ve told you: I’ll get hold of old Bita, and get her to rustle you up a nice well-stacked little tart, and the four of us could really live it up during this Carnival.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: But this is the last day of Carnival.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Then we’ll live it up during Lent, while the bosses are day-dreaming in church listening to the sermons. Hey, hang on! Old Gherardo’s front door is opening. Stay back here, out of sight.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: What for?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Just in case.

div2.stage: (Isabella and Lelia appear on the doorstep of Gherardo’s house.)

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Now listen, Isabella, don’t forget what you’ve promised me.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: And you don’t forget to come and see me again. Wait, come here, I want to tell you something.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: If I were in the place of that pansy, I’d show the boss a trick or two!

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: You’d taste the goods yourself before you delivered them, eh?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: You can say that again.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Is that all, then?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Listen a moment.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What now?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Is there anyone out there who can see us?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I can’t see a soul.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: What the hell is she after?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: A bit over-familiar, I’d say.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Let’s see.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Here a moment.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: They’re getting a bit close to each other.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: So they are. I wonder....

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: You know, I wish....

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What do you wish?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: I wish... Come nearer.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Go on, nearer, you great bumpkin!

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: See if there’s anyone there.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I told you, there’s nobody.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: I wish you could come back after dinner, when my father has gone out.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: All right, I will: but when my master passes by here, you must run indoors and shut the window in his face.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: If I don’t do just that, never love me more.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Here, where’s she putting her hand?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: (gleefully) Well poor old Flamminio! I told him, didn’t I? I must have second sight.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Good-bye.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Wait, must you go?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Kiss her, pox rot you!

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: He’s afraid someone will see.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Shouldn’t you get back indoors now?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Please, I want a favour from you.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Step inside the door a moment.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: They’re off!

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: You’re very shy.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Someone will see us.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Hey, hey, hey hey! Holy smoke! How about one for me, now?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: I told you he’d kiss her.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: And I’m telling you I’d rather have seen that kiss, with you as witness, than earn a hundred crowns.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: I saw it, all right! I wish I’d felt it too.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Now what is the boss going to do when he finds out?

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Bloody hell! You’re not going to tell him?

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Forgive me. You’re too handsome, and I love you too much, so I’ve done what I shouldn’t, and perhaps now you’ll despise me. But God knows I couldn’t hold back any longer.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: You need not explain yourself to me, my lady; I know how it is with me too, and how much I have been led to do by too much love.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: What have you done?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: What? Oh... I have deceived my master, and it is not right.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: To hell with your master!

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: And that’s what you get for trusting a tart! It serves him right. No wonder the snooty little fop was trying to persuade him to give her up.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: The Lord helps those who help themselves — and he’s helping himself with a vengeance! They’re all the same, these women, when you get down to it.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: It’s late, and I have to find my master. God be with you.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Wait.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Wheeee! And one for luck! You wait, my pretty boy, it won’t taste so nice in an hour or two!

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: (adjusting his dress) Jesus Christ, I’ve grown an extra leg!

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Lock the door, now. Good-bye.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Do what you like with me!

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I’m all yours. (Isabella goes in and shuts the door.) I don’t know what I’m going to do. On the one hand I’m having the time of my life, bamboozling that silly wench into thinking I’m a man; on the other hand, I’m getting into a mess, and I don’t know how to get out of it. She’s got as far as kissing now, and she’ll try to go further when she gets the chance; and that will expose my weak point, and the whole trick will fall apart. I must get to Clemenzia and ask her what I ought to do next. But there’s Flamminio coming.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Listen, Stoke, the boss said he’d wait for me at the Porrini Exchange. I’m going to give him this piece of good news. If he doesn’t believe me, you must back me up and say I’m not a liar.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: All right, I owe you a favour. But if I were you, I’d keep quiet about it. You’ll have it as a hold over Fabio, and he’ll have to let you do whatever you want.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: No, you’ve got it all wrong. I can’t stand the bastard, he’s ruined me with the boss.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Do as you like then.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Is it possible, though, that I have so little control and so little self-respect that I insist on loving that woman against her will? Dancing attendance on someone who torments me, who ignores me, who won’t even favour me with a glance? Am I so soft and spiritless that I cannot rid myself of this shame and this suffering? But there is Fabio. Well, what have you managed to achieve?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Why did you take so long? You’re getting to be as bad as those other layabouts.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I had to wait around to try and speak to Isabella.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Then why didn’t you speak to her?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Because she wouldn’t listen. And if you were to take my advice, you’d cut your losses and turn your mind elsewhere; because, from what I’ve been able to gather so far, you are wasting your time. She is determined not to do a single thing that you want.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I won’t give in, I don’t care who says so! Do you know, I was passing by there just now, and the moment she saw me she leapt up from the window with such fury and contempt that you’d think she’d seen something horrible or frightening.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Let her go, I tell you. Is it possible that in all this city there can be no one who deserves your love as well as she does? Have you never loved anyone else?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: If only I had not! I’m afraid that this might be the cause of all my troubles. Because I told you, I was very much in love once before with that girl Lelia, Virginio Bellenzini’s daughter. I’m afraid that Isabella suspects that this affair is still going on, and that’s why she won’t look at me. But I shall make it clear that I don’t love Lelia any longer — I hate her, in fact, I can’t bear to hear her mentioned. I’ll make any promise Isabella wants never to go near her again. You can go and tell her so.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Aaaah!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What’s the matter? You look as if you’re going to faint. What is it?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Ahi!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Where does it hurt?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Ahi! My heart!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How long have you been feeling it? Lean on me a moment. Have you hurt yourself somewhere?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: No, sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Does your stomach feel weak?

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: No sir, I said it’s my heart that hurts.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: So does mine, my poor boy, even more! You’re quite pale. Go straight home, get a warm cloth put against your chest, and have yourself rubbed down: that’s probably all you need. I’ll be there quite soon, and if it’s necessary I’ll get a doctor to come and feel your pulse and see what’s wrong. Give me your arm a moment. You’re frozen. Go along now, and take it easy. (Lelia begins to go.) What a strange thing to happen! I wouldn’t want to lose this lad, not for anything in the world. I’ve never known a servant as capable or so well-bred; and what is more, he seems so attached to me that if he were a woman I’d think he was in love with me. — Fabio, go on home, I tell you, and get yourself warm. I’ll be there soon. Tell them to get the meal ready.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Now you’ve heard, haven’t you, heard with your own ears, from his own ungrateful mouth, how much Flamminio loves you! Poor Lelia, miserable Lelia! Why do you still waste time adoring this unfeeling beast? Your patience has been of no use, nor have your prayers, nor have the favours you have shown him; and now trickery is of no use either. Look at me now! Refused, rejected, avoided, hated! Why do I seek out a man who refuses me? Why do I offer myself to a man who rejects me? Why do I seek out a man who avoids me? Why do I love a man who detests me? Flamminio! You only have eyes for Isabella. He only wants Isabella. He can have her then, he can keep her; I shall give him up, or else die. I am resolved, since he hates me so much, never to serve him again in these clothes, and never to appear in his sight. I shall go and find Clemenzia, I know she’s waiting in her house; and I’ll let her decide what is to become of me.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: If I’m not telling you the truth, you can cut my tongue out, you can have me hanged if you like. I swear to you, that was how it was!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How long ago?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: When you sent me to look for him.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Now tell me the whole thing again from the beginning, because he says he wasn’t even allowed to speak to her.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Well he’s not going to admit it, is he? I’ve told you: I was spying to see if he was hanging round her house, and I saw him come out of it. He was just about to leave, and Isabella called him back in again. They looked to see if there was anyone outside who could see them, didn’t see anybody, and started kissing each other.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How was it they didn’t see you?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I’d slipped back into that porch opposite. They couldn’t see me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How could you see, then?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: With my eyes. What do you think I saw them with, my elbows?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: And you say he kissed her?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I don’t know if she kissed him or he kissed her, but I reckon one of them kissed the other.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Were their faces close enough for them to kiss each other?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I don’t know about their faces. Their lips were.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What does that mean? Could they put their lips close to each other without their faces?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Well, I suppose they could if their mouths were in their ears or their necks, but otherwise... no.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You’d better be sure of what you saw. Don’t come later saying ‘Well, I think I saw them....’ This is a really big matter, you know.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I’ve seen bigger things. There’s that giant that rings the bell on the tower in Siena....

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How did you see them?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: By being awake, with my eyes open, hanging around to see and with nothing to do but look.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: If it’s true, you’ve been the death of me.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: It is true. She called him, she stepped close to him, she hugged him, she kissed him. So if you want to die, then die.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: No wonder the traitor said he’d never been inside! Now I know why the little filth kept urging me to leave her: so he could enjoy her himself. By God, if I’m any sort of a man, I’ll make such an example of him that no servant will cheat his master again as long as this town stands! But I’m not going to believe you until there’s some other proof. You’re a bad lot yourself, and you’ve got it in for Fabio – you’d do this to make me get rid of him. But by the holy God above, I’ll get the truth out of you or kill you. Come on, now! You really saw this?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Yes sir.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: He kissed her?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: They kissed each other.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How many times?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Twice.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: In her hallway.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You’re lying in your teeth. Just now you said in the doorway.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I meant near the doorway.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Tell the truth!

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Ahi, ahi! I wish I hadn’t told you anything!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Was it the truth?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Yes sir. But I forgot, there was a witness.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Who was that?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Stoke, Virginio’s servant.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Did he see all this too?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Just like I did.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: And suppose he won’t admit it?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Then you can kill me.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I shall.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: And if he does admit it?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Then I’ll kill both....

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: No! Why?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I don’t mean you two — Isabella and Fabio.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: And burn the whole house down, with Pasquella and the rest inside!

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: We’ll go and find Stoke. If I don’t pay him out.... I won’t have it said.... the whole town will see if I.... I’ll have such a revenge! The traitor! That’s what comes of trusting....

div2.head: Scene 1
div2.stage: FABRIZIO, Virginio’s young son (the image of Lelia); MASTER PETER, his tutor; SQUINT, their servant

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: This city seems completely altered since I was here last. Mind you, I was only passing through with the legation from Ancona, and we stayed at the Guicciardini Inn. But we did stay for about a week. Do you recognize any part of it, Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I might just as well never have set foot here.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Well, of course, you were so little when you left, it’s not surprising, is it? But I think I do recognize this street. That’s the Rangoni palace; this is where the great canal goes underneath; and look, there’s the Cathedral at the end. See? And you know they call their Town Hall the Mayory — so there’s that saying about a person who thinks a lot of himself, ‘He thinks he’s the Hairy Mayory of Modena’.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Of course. Is it here?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Take a look up there, on the Cathedral.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Is that the Hairy Mayory?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That’s right.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: But it’s a joke!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Well, there you are then.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What’s that other saying — ‘taking the bear to Modena’, for going on a wild goose chase? What does that mean? What bear is it?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Those are venerable proverbs de quibus nescitur origo — of which the origin is not known.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Do you know, Master Peter, there’s something about this city which agrees with me.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: And there’s something that agrees with me, too. I can smell some meat roasting somewhere, that’s making my mouth water.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (ignoring Squint) Well, what did my old teacher Cantalicius say? ‘ Dulcis amor patriae ’ — sweet is the love of one’s own homeland. And Cato too: ‘ Pugna pro patria ’ — fight for your country. Hic, haec, hoc . When all is said and done, there’s nothing sweeter than home.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Oh yes there is, teacher — Trebbiano wine. And I could do with a flagon of it right now. I’m getting a dropped shoulder carrying this trunk.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: These streets must be newly paved. When I was here last, they were all filthy and muddy.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Are we going to stand around here and count the bricks? It’ll take some time. How about shifting ourselves, double quick, to somewhere where we can have some dinner?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (primly) Iamdudum animus est in patinis — his soul is already among the saucepans.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What’s that coat of arms with those gimlets on?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That’s the badge of the Commune, they call it the Screw. Just as in Florence they use the Marzocco lion as their rallying cry, and in Venice they rally to St. Mark, and in Siena to the emblem of the she-wolf, here in Modena they rally round the Screw.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: I’d rather we started thinking about rallying round the Stew.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I know that one: it’s the arms of the Duke.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Hey teacher, it’s your turn to carry the luggage. I’m so parched I can hardly talk.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Don’t worry, you'll get your drink soon enough.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: When I’m dead, which won’t be long at this rate, you’ll be able to boil an egg in my gurgling guts.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Well anyway, judging by first impressions, I really like this city. How about you, Squint?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Oh yes, master, it’s just like being in Paradise among the angels — nobody ever seems to need food and drink. Come on, now! Don’t let’s waste any more time sight-seeing, there’ll be plenty of chances for that later.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: The Cathedral here has the most superb bell-tower you could possibly find in the compass of this world.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Is that the one the citizens wanted to make a cover for, a sort of sheath? The one that's supposed to turn you mad if you stand in its shadow?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That is correct.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: In that case, I’m not setting foot outside the kitchen. You can go and see it, if you're that daft. Now let’s find somewhere to stay.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: You’re in a great hurry!

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Poxing hell, I’m dying of hunger! All I’ve eaten today was a half chicken that someone left in the river boat.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Should we ask somebody to show us where my father’s house is?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: No. I think we should find accommodation at a hostelry first, settle down, and then try and trace him at our leisure.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: As you wish. This must be where the inns are.

div2.head: Scene 2
div2.stage: FABRIZIO; MASTER PETER; SQUINT; two innkeepers, EASY and WHISK

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Well now, gentlemen! If you’re looking for lodging, here is the very place! At the sign of the Looking Glass!

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Welcome back to Modena! You’ve stayed with me before, haven't you? Don’t you remember your old friend Whisk, at your service as always? Come along in, gentlemen, all travellers of your standing lodge here.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Why not come and lodge with me? I can offer good rooms, a good fire, excellent beds and fresh linen. You’ll not go short of anything you’ve got....

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: I should hope not!

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Er... that is, of anything you want.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: I can give you the best wine in Lombardy, nice plump partridges, good solid salami, pigeons, chickens and whatever else you ask for — you'll be able to feast yourselves.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: That’s what I’m after!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (to Easy) And what do you say?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: I can give you calves’ sweetbreads, mortadella, fine mountain wine — all the choicest, most delicate fare there is.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: If you come to me, you’ll get less delicacy and more food. I’ll feast you like lords, and leave you to set a fair price. If you go to the Looking Glass, he’ll charge you separately for every candle you use. It’s up to you.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (to Fabrizio) Let’s go here, boss, it’s better.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Come to me, if you want proper treatment. Do you want people to know that you’re lodging at the sign of the Fool’s Cap?

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: My Fool’s Cap is a hundred times better than your Mirror!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Speculum Prudentiae significat: ‘Nosce teipsum’ . Do you follow me, Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Yes: ‘The mirror of Prudence teaches us to know ourselves’.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: (to Easy) Who gets the most custom — you or me?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: But who gets the best custom, the people of quality?

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Where are they fed better?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Where are they nourished more delicately?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: What’s all this ‘delicate’ rubbish all the time? What I want is more food for my belly, and less of this ‘delicate’ stuff. All this finicky eating is for ruddy Florentines.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Indeed, sir, the Florentine travellers always stay with me.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: They used to, you mean. For the last three years they’ve been coming to me instead.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: (to Squint) Come now, my good man, why don't you put that trunk down in here? It must be breaking your back.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Don’t worry about me. I’m not resting my back until I can be sure of my belly.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Would a pair of capons suit you? (Calls inside) Bring them out! These can be just for you.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: No, really? Well, perhaps just for starters.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Look at the colour of this ham, gentlemen, it’s like crimson silk!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (acting the conoisseur) Not bad at all.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Who’s the expert on wine?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: I am — better than any Frenchman.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Taste this, and see if it appeals to you. If not, I can offer you a dozen others.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Whisk, my old mate, I like your style. That other fellow sets you up to drink before he even knows which wine is right for you. (Tastes the wine) Oh boss, it’s great! (To Whisk) Here you are, in with the trunk.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Not quite so hasty. (To Easy) What have you to say?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: I say that gentlemen of quality do not wish simply to eat as much as they can. They eat modestly, and choose only the best.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: He sounds as if he’s running a workhouse, or a hospital.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (To Easy) I like your words, friend. What can you offer us?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Anything you choose.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: I’m surprised at you gentlemen. When the supply is plentiful, a man can eat as little or as much as he likes: if there is only a little to start with, he hasn’t got the same choice. And then, once you have started, your appetite often turns out to be greater than you thought, and you need to fill up the corners with bread.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Impeccable logic! Spoken like a judge! I never saw a man who understood me so well. Whisk, you and me are blood brothers.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Just step into the kitchen then, brother, and have a look round.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Omnis repletio mala, panis autem pessima — All satiety is harmful, but that of bread is worst.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Pedantic poof! I’ll knock your teeth in one day, if I live long enough.

div2.stage: (He goes into the kitchen of the Fool’s Cap.)

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Why not come inside, gentlemen? It’s not wise to stand about in the cold.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Oh come now, we’re not such easy freezers as that.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: I must tell you gentlemen that the Looking Glass Inn used to be the best house in Lombardy. But since I opened up under the sign of the Fool’s Cap, he doesn’t get more than a dozen clients a year, and my sign is now more famous throughout the world than any other inn you can name. The French come here in droves, and the Germans too, to a man.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: That’s a lie: all Germans lodge at the sign of the Pig-Sty.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: I get all the trade from Milan, from Parma, from Piacenza....

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: And I get all the trade from Venice, from Genoa, from Florence....

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Where do the Neapolitans lodge?

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: With me.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Rubbish. Most of them go to the Bed of Venus.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: There’s still plenty who come to me.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Where does the Duke of Amalfi lodge?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: Sometimes at my place, sometimes at his; sometimes at the sign of the Sword, and sometimes at the Bed of Venus. Just as his lordship pleases.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: We come from Rome: where do the Romans stay?

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: They come to me.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: That’s a lie. You won’t find a single one there from one year’s end to the next. Or rather, it’s true that some of the older Cardinals still go there out of habit; but all the newer ones head straight for the Fool’s Cap.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (emerging) I’m not stirring out of here, not even if you carry me. These two can go where they like. Boss, you should see inside the kitchen. (Rhapsodical) There’s loads of pots all round the fire, full of everything you can think of: soups and sauces and gravies, and there’s spits full of partridges and thrushes and pigeons, roast kid, capon boiled, roast and stewed, marinades, pastries, pies — you’d think they were expecting a second Carnival, or the Pope’s whole household for the night.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Have you had a drink yet?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: And the wines, boss, the wines...!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Variorum ciborum commistio pessimam generat digestionem — A mixture of various commestibles causes gross indigestion.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (furious) Horum scorum cretinorum fetchat cloutat lug-holibus! What a wet bloody blanket you are! The pox rot you, and all the rest of you schoolmasters! You’re about as cheerful as the municipal hangman. Come on, boss, let’s go inside.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Where do the Spaniards lodge?

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: I don’t get mixed up with that lot. They can stay where they belong, at the sign of the Fiddle. But we don’t need to chatter any longer. There isn’t a traveller on the road who doesn’t rest under this sign here. Except the folk from Siena, of course, who count as honorary citizens of Modena, and have a dozen friends to put them up at home the moment they arrive in town. Otherwise, lords and masters, rich and poor, soldiers and gay companions, all come running to the sign of the Fool’s Cap.

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: But the learned doctors, the judges, the friars, and all virtuous men come under my sign.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: And yet it’s surprising how, after a few days, some of those who started off at the Looking Glass change their minds, and come over to stay with me.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What shall we do, sir?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Etiam atque etiam cogitandum — this must be pondered again and again.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (an idea dawning) I’ve got it! Look out, stomach, here it comes. This time there’ll be no mistake....

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: It seems to me, Fabrizio, that we’re on the brink of penury...

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Professor! The host over here has got a beautiful little boy, chubby as a cherub.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (fatally tempted, changes his mind in a split second) Well, let’s stay here. Your father will be able to pay the bill, if we find him.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Hooked him just in time. It's his weakness, it never fails. Three drinks already, and look at me. I shan’t leave that kitchen till I’ve tasted everything in it, and then I’ll sleep it off by that beautiful fire. And to hell with saving for your old age!

div2.stage: (They enter under the sign of the Fool’s Cap.)

sp.speaker: EASY
sp.p: You’d better watch it, Whisk. You’re being too clever for your own good. One of these days you’ll find yourself in a punch-up.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Whenever you like, sunshine. It can’t be too soon for me.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (in anguished fury) Is this the way you taught her to behave? Is this the honour she does to my name? I’m the most unlucky man alive! I survive one disaster after another, and what do I find at the end of it all? I see my property without an heir! I see my household scattered, and my daughter a whore! Am I to be the laughing stock of all the riff-raff in town? Will I never hold up my head again in company? Must I be sniggered at by urchins, mocked by old men, put in plays by Sienese Academics, made an example of in stories, and have my name bandied about by every woman in Modena? They’re the biggest gossips in Italy, they’ll slaughter me with their tongues. They must all have heard by now: it only needs one to find out, and it’ll be all round the town in a couple of hours. Why did I have children? Why do I live so long, just to end with all this grief? I don’t know what to do; I don’t know which way to turn.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: The best thing you can do is to make as little noise about it as you can, and do your best to see that she gets back home before the whole town finds out. But in any case, I’m sure that that Sister Chattery Charity wasn’t telling the truth — and I hope she chokes to death on her own lying tongue. Lelia going about in man’s clothes, indeed! Mark my words, they’re just making this all up so you’ll have to make her a nun, and leave all your property to the convent.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: What do you mean, not telling the truth? She had all the details, she even told me that Lelia’s taken service with a gentleman of this town, and that he hasn’t realized yet that she’s a woman.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, the oddest things happen, I suppose — but really, I can’t believe a word of it.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Nor can I believe that he doesn’t know she’s a woman.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: That wasn’t what I meant.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: It’s what I meant, though; and I’m the one who has to suffer. Though I suppose it’s my own fault, giving her to you to nurse — I knew well enough what sort of woman you are.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: That’s enough of that, Virginio. If I’ve been something less than I should be, it was you who made me so. You know quite well that until you came along I’d never been with anyone except my husband. What I say is that you never knew how to treat a young girl like Lelia. Weren’t you ashamed at trying to marry her off to that death’s head old enough to be her grandfather?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: And what’s wrong with old men, you female thug? They’re a sight better than young ones.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: You’re losing your grip, you know. People are beginning to spot you a mile off. No wonder they’re feeding you all sorts of tall stories, like this one....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: If I find her, I’ll drag her back home through the streets by her hair!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: That’s right: instead of keeping your shame under your cloak, you’ll stick it up there on your forehead for all to see.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I don’t care. Everyone is going to know in any case. I’ll wash it off again by giving her the punishment she deserves.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, do it your way, then. It won’t be your head that hurts.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I know exactly what she’s wearing, I’ve got all the details. I’m going to keep on looking until I find her. Then she’ll get what’s coming.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Just as you like. I’m going, I can see I’m wasting my breath. All the same....

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: (They emerge from the inn. Fabrizio has taken off his travel clothes, and is dressed more like ‘Fabio’.)

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: While my two men are resting, I’m going to look round the town. When they get up, tell them to come in the direction of the main square.

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: You know, young master, if I hadn’t actually seen you put those clothes on, I would have sworn you were a lad from this town — a gentleman’s servant, who wears white like you are now, and is the spitting image of you.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: (joking) He must be a long lost brother of mine!

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Could be indeed, sir.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Can you tell my tutor to start looking around for the man we’ve come to see?

sp.speaker: WHISK
sp.p: Leave it to me, sir.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Bless me, there he is. I was afraid I’d have to tramp all round the town before I found him. Fabio! Thank goodness you’re here. I was coming to look for you, and you’ve saved me the trouble. Listen, sweetie, my mistress says can you come and see her now about something very important to you both. I can’t think what it can be.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Who is your mistress?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: As if you don’t know. I must say it was a stroke of luck coming across you like this.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I’ve not ‘come across’ anyone here yet: but if she’ll come across for me, I’ll come across her.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: There’s no spunk in either of you. I wish I was young again and had your chance to make a meal of things. If I were in your shoes, I’d have done with all your suspicions and scruples long ago. But you’ll make it in the end.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I think your ladyship has got the wrong end of the stick. Run along, will you? You’ve mistaken me for someone else.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Come on, Fabio my love, don’t go all offended. I’m only trying to help you along.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I’m not offended at anything — but that’s not my name, so I can’t be who you think.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh, do as you like then, the pair of you. But do you know what, sonny? There are very few to compare with her in this town, either for looks or for money. And I just wish you’d both stop dithering and get down to business: because the more I have to go chasing back and forth every day, bringing messages and taking answers, the more people are going to talk. And that won’t help either your pleasure or her reputation.

p.seg: What’s all this story, then? I can’t make it out. Either she’s off her head, or she’s got the wrong man. All the same, I’d like to see where it all leads.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (at the door of Gherardo’s house) Wait! I think there’s someone inside. Wait around for a minute, and I’ll see if Isabella is on her own. If there’s no one, I’ll wave you to come in.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I’m going to see how this fairy-tale is supposed to end. Perhaps she works for some fancy whore, and thinks she’s going to wheedle a pile of ducats out of me. If that’s so, she's got a shock coming — after my apprenticeship with the Spaniards, so to speak, I’m more likely to charge her five than pay her three. One of us is going to wind up the loser, that’s for sure. I’ll stand away from the house a bit, and watch who comes in and out, to see what type of woman she is.

div2.head: Scene 6
div2.stage:
GHERARDO; VIRGINIO; [two Servants "Servants"
two Servants : These are not mentioned in the stage direction. But someone (in the plural) will be asked to guard Fabrizio in Scene 7. It makes most sense that those people should be Pluck and Stoke. — PLUCK and STOKE?]; PASQUELLA reappearing later on the doorstep

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: No thank you very much. If that’s the way things are, you can keep her. If your daughter has done a thing like that, then the very least I can think is that she did it because she doesn’t want me. But it’s more likely that she’s already taken someone else.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: But it’s not true, Gherardo. Don’t you think I would have told you? Please don’t spoil everything we’ve arranged.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’d ask you not to mention it again.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Aren’t you going to honour our bargain?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Not if you’re supplying shop-soiled goods. In any case, you don’t even know if you’ll get her back: you’re trying to sell the bird while it’s still on the bush. I heard it all, when you were talking to Clemenzia — everything.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: All right: if I don’t find her again, I won’t insist. But if I do find her, won’t you agree to a wedding straight away?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Virginio, my first wife was the most respected lady in this whole city, and my daughter is as pure as a lamb. Do you think I’m going to bring into such a household a girl who has run away from her father, and who is going round other people’s houses dressed as a man, like some unmentionable trollop? Can’t you see that once I did that, I’d never find a husband for Isabella?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: It’ll all blow over after a few days. It’s not as bad as you think. No one knows about it except you and I.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: And before you can turn round, the whole town will know too.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: That’s not true.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (wavering slightly) How long is it since she disappeared?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Only yesterday or this morning.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I hope you’re right. But are you sure she’s still in Modena?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Well, find her, and we’ll talk about it again.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Do you promise you’ll have her?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’ll see.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Give me your word now....

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Not now, but....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Please, Gherardo! Now, in all sincerity....

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Not so hasty! Pasquella, what are you doing there? Where’s Isabella?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: She’s praying to her little altar, as usual.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: The blessed angel! What a consolation to have a daughter who’s always on her knees! She’s an absolute treasure.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh you’re so right! You wouldn’t believe how she fasts and stays awake all night, like a little saint. Her hands are never away from her beads.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Just like her poor dear mother, may she rest in Paradise!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It’s the gospel truth. When I think of the good works that poor lady did.... She used to flagellate herself more, and wear more hairy shirts, than any woman I've ever known. And so charitable to others! If it had been up to her, she’d have taken in every passing friar, every priest, every wandering beggar who came to the door, and given them all she’d got. It was only her respect for your property, sir, that held her back.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: She had remarkable qualities.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Do you know, she used to get up one hour, even two hours before dawn, to go and hear the early mass along with the friars at St. Francis’. She went by night so as not to attract attention, so she wouldn’t be thought a hippogriff, like some sanctimonious show-offs I could mention.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: What do you mean, a ‘hippogriff’?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I’ve never heard that word before.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’m sure that’s what she used to say.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: You mean ‘hypocrite’, don’t you?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Maybe that’s it. But she’ll be outdone by her daughter, you mark my words.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let us pray that she will.

div2.stage: (At this point Virginio catches sight of Fabrizio, to whom Pasquella may have been signalling meanwhile.)

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Ssssst! Gherardo! Gherardo! Over there... it’s her... the, er, woman we were talking about before! Oh the shame of it! She’s seen me, and she doesn’t even try to hid or run away. Let’s get her.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Are you sure you aren’t mistaken? Perhaps it isn’t her after all.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Of course it’s her! She’s dressed just as sister Chattery said she would be.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: This is going all wrong. I think I’m for it.

div2.head: Scene 7

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Well good day to you, my young miss! Is this your idea of suitable clothing? A real credit to the family, aren’t you? A real consolation and support to your poor old father! I wish I’d dropped dead the moment I conceived you, rather than see you born to bury me alive under such shame. What do you think, eh, Gherardo? What do you think of your bride? A fine spectacle, isn’t she?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Not so fast with the ‘bride’ — I haven’t said....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: You wicked little slut! It would serve you right if this gentleman were to refuse you now, and break off the match. But he’s being generous enough to overlook your insane behaviour, and he’ll marry you just the same.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Now wait a minute!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Get home this minute, you wretch! I wish I’d never got you, nor your mother ever nourished you, if this is what it was to lead to.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Tell me, old gentleman, haven’t you any sons, or relatives, or friends in this town who ought to be looking after you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Look how she answers me back! What are you talking about?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Because, seeing that you so obviously need the attentions of a doctor, I’m surprised they let you out of the house. Anywhere else they’d keep you locked up.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I should have locked you up long ago, hussy, and skinned you alive into the bargain. Bring me a knife, someone — I’ll do it now!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Old man, you clearly don’t know me very well, and perhaps you think you can abuse me as you like because I’m a foreigner. But as it happens I’m from Modena myself, and my father is as good a man and as well born as you are.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (to himself) She’s pretty, at least. If she hasn’t gone too far, I might decide to have her after all.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: And just why did you run away from this father of yours, and from the place where I had lodged you?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I can’t remember you ever lodging me anywhere. As for leaving my father, I had no choice.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Oh, really? And who forced you?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: The Spanish soldiers.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (blenching) And where have you come from now?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: From their camp.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: From the soldiers’ camp?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: That’s right.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: The whole thing is off.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Then damn you to hell!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Your words on your own head!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Gherardo, please, let’s get her into your house, so nobody sees her like this.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Not me. Take her to your own house.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: For the sake of our friendship, open up the door.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: No, I tell you.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Listen here a moment. And you two (to the servants) make sure she doesn’t go away.

div2.stage: (He takes Gherardo aside, to confer with him.)

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: (to audience) I’ve known plenty of people from Modena, and they were all a bit cracked; but I’ve never seen anyone as mad as this old fool, who wasn’t locked up and chained to the wall. And the queer way it takes him! As far as I can see, his madness makes him mistake young men for women. It’s even better than Molza’s story of the Sienese woman, whose head was so empty she thought it was a sponge — because when all is said and done, women aren’t supposed to have much sense to start with, whereas old men ought by rights to have picked up some wisdom. I shall be able to dine out on this story when Carnival comes round again. They’re coming back. Let’s see what they’ve got to say.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (returning) To tell you the honest truth, I’m still very much in two minds. Let’s find out exactly what she has done and what she hasn’t.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (to Fabrizio) Come here.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What can I do for you, old man?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: You’re a sordid wretch.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Watch your tongue. I’m not going to put up with insults.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: You brazen minx!

div2.stage: (He lays hands on Fabrizio, who reacts violently in his turn. Gherardo and the servants intervene.)

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Hey, hey, hey!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (to Fabrizio) Don’t be so touchy, now! Can’t you see he's just lost his temper? Humour him a little.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What does he want with me? What have I got to do with him, or with you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Have you still got the impudence to answer me? Whose child do you think you are?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Virginio Bellenzini’s.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: And I wish to God you weren’t. You’re sending me to an early grave.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: An early grave, at your age? You’re lucky to have lived so long. You can call it a day whenever you like, as far as I’m concerned: you seem to have outstayed your welcome.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Only because of you, you trollop!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Words like that don’t solve anything. Come now, my fine young miss, that’s not the way to address your father.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: They’re breeding like rabbits! Two of them now, with exactly the same disease. This is getting ridiculous.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Laughing now, are you?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: It’s not a good sign, you know, to be mocking your father.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: What have ‘father’ or ‘mother’ got to do with it? My father was Virginio, my mother was Giovanna, and that’s all the parents I ever had. You must be off your head! Do you think I’m completely alone in this town, with no friends to fall back on?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Virginio, do you know what I’m beginning to think? That perhaps this poor young lady’s brains have been disturbed by too much brooding.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (almost eagerly) I’m afraid you’re right. I thought there was something odd right from the start, from the way she shrugged me off like that.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (retreating) Ah, but that could have a different explanation.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Once a woman has lost her virtue, there’s nothing left to restrain her.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I think it’s more likely that her wits are a bit deranged.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: The odd thing is that she knows her parents’ names, but doesn’t recognize you face to face.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Let’s get her inside your house, since it’s close at hand. I couldn’t get her all the way back home without the whole town seeing us.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: (emerging from some unspecified business with the servants) What are those two drooling old Methuselahs up to?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Let’s humour her gently until we get her inside the house; then we can grab her, and shut her in with your daughter.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Right, that’s the plan then.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Come along then, my treasure! I can’t stay angry with you for long. I’ll forgive and forget everything, as long as you behave decently in future.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: That’s a good girl, then.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Here comes the second clown, right on cue.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Well now! It won’t do you any good to stand around chatting dressed like that. Come along inside, now. Pasquella! Open up, please.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Come inside now, daughter.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I would prefer not to.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I would rather not enter the house of a man whom I do not know.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (ironic) Well now, what a fine sense of womanly modesty!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Didn’t I say she was virtuous, as well as beautiful?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Yes — she dresses with such restraint, too!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (to Fabrizio) I only want a little word with you.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Say it out here.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Come now, this isn’t proper. This is not a stranger’s house, it’s your house too, since you’re going to be my wife.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Your wife? Why, you dirty old bu... buffer!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Your father has made all the arrangements.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Do you think I’m some rotten little queen who lets just anybody...?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Come now, forget it. Don’t let’s make her angry. Listen, my angel: I shan’t make you do anything you don’t want.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Listen, old fellow, you’ve got the wrong idea about me.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Let’s have a word about it — indoors.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Well, why not? A dozen words, if you like. After all, why should I be afraid of you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Gherardo, now you’ve got her in, let’s arrange to shut her in the bedroom with your daughter, until we can send for her proper clothes.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Just as you like, old friend. Pasquella! Bring the key of the downstairs bedroom, and call Isabella to come down.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: It would serve you right if he took you out and beat you black and blue! Then you would learn to stay with him and look after him when he goes out, and not to get drunk and doze off as you did, and let him wander away by himself.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: And he ought to take you out and cover you with pitch and brimstone, faggots and gunpowder, and set light to you! That would teach you not to be the pervert that you are.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Drunken hog!

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Ped... ped... pedant!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Wait until I tell the young master!

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Wait until I tell his father!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: And just what do you intend to tell his father?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: What will you say about me?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That you’re a wastrel, a hooligan, a vagabond, a delinquent, a maniac, and a drunkard. Is that enough?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: And I’ll say that you’re a thief, a gambler, a muck-raker, a cheat, a swindler, a quack, a boaster, a bonehead, a bigmouth, an ignoramus, a double-crosser, and a filthy sodomite. Is that enough?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: So now we know.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Too right we do.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I’ve nothing more to say. It’s beneath my dignity to bandy words with the likes of you.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: My God yes! I was forgetting your high-class origins. The bluest blood in Fairyland! You know damn well your father was a mule-driver, you’re even more of a peasant than I am. Look at him, for God’s sake: just because he’s learned how to say ‘ quia masculinus sum ’, he thinks he can lord it over the lot of us.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: ‘Philosophy, thou art reduced to rags.’ Who would have thought to hear the language of divine learning — lingua latina — issue from the jaws of an ass?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You’ll be the ass, if you don’t change your tune — because I’ll be weighing your back down with sticks.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Take care, Squint, there is an end to the patience even of a philosopher: furor fit laesa saepius sapientia . One day I could lose my temper. Now let me alone, you stable-scullion, lout and arch-lout!

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Pedant, arch-pedant, pedantextra, pedantissimo! Is there anything worse than being a pedant? Is there a worse race of scum, or a lousier occupation under the sun? They swan around with their heads swollen like bladders, just because of being called ‘Master This’ and ‘Doctor That’; and if they see a hat being taken off half a mile away, they think it’s meant for them and salute back. Oh your very humble servant, Master Bowel, Master Turd, Doctor Squitters, Master Shitface!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Tractant fabrilia fabri . Workmen carry their own tools with them. One can see that you’re descending to your own proper level.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: It’s a level that always seems to interest you.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Get out — you’re blocking my passage.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You’ve never managed to ‘block my passage’, have you? Though it’s not been for want of trying.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I’ll be....

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (interrupting) And I'll C! It’s no use threatening me, sweetheart! There’s not a single piece of filth you’ve got up to that I don’t know about, and I could have you tied to a stake any time I choose. So stop trying to bugger me about.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I have no desire to do any such thing. What do you take me for?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Then I must be the first one you haven’t fancied.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Listen, Squint, either you leave this household or I will.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Come off it! How many times have you said that before? You wouldn’t leave this set-up if they rode you out on a broomstick. Where else would you find such a tasty young lad, who’ll eat with you and study with you and sleep with you like this one here?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Heavens, as though I would be short of offers, if I chose to take them! There are people who are begging for my services!

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Make way for the belle of the ball! Join the queue for the next dance!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: We’d better stop this right now. Go back to the inn, and look after the master’s things. We’ll settle our accounts later.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: I’ll go back to the inn all right — and perhaps I’ll open an account in your name, which you’ll have to pay. (They separate.) If I didn’t give that bastard a scare from time to time, I wouldn’t be able to stand living with him. He’s as timid as a rabbit. If I stand up to him, he daren’t say a word: but if I were to let him get on top of me, he’d pin me down with the weight of his erudition. It’s a good job I know what he’s like.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: As far as dowry is concerned, we’ll stick to our bargain. I’ll endow her as you please, and you add a thousand florins if your son doesn’t turn up.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Agreed.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: If I’m not mistaken, I’ve seen that gentleman before — but I can’t think where.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: What are you staring at, my good man?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Can it be my old master?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let him gawp as he pleases. He’s probably a stranger here. In other towns they don’t seem to mind being stared at, and everyone’s allowed to look as he likes.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: If I am staring, sir, it is not sine causa, without good cause. Tell me, do either of you know Virginio Bellenzini, a citizen of this town?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
