sp.p: Yes, I know him. In fact I’m the closest friend he’s got. But what do you want with him? If you’re hoping to lodge with him, I can tell you that he has other things on his mind, and won’t have time for you, so it would be better to look elsewhere.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But surely you yourself are the very man. Salvete, patronorum optime!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Can you be Master Peter Hayseed, my son’s tutor?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: The very same.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Oh my poor son! What news have you of him? Where did you leave him? Where did he die? Why have you been so long bringing the news? Did they kill him, those treacherous heathen swine? My poor son! All I had in the world! Tell me, please, quickly, my dear tutor!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Don’t weep, master, please.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Gherardo! Son-in-law! Here is the man who tutored my poor dear son while he was alive. Dear Master Peter! My poor, poor boy — where is he buried? Do you know? Won’t you tell me? I’m caught between longing to know and fear of hearing it spoken.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But master, don’t cry. Why are you crying?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Shouldn’t I weep for that sweet young boy? So quick and clever, so beautifully mannered? And those swine killed him!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: God forbid! Your son is alive and well.

p.seg: That's bad news for me, if it’s true. I stand to lose a thousand florins.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Alive and well? Can it be? But if that were true, he’d be with you now.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Virginio, do you really know this man? Might he not be some kind of swindler?

p.emph: Parcius ista viris, tamen obiicienda memento!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Eh?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Your insinuations, sir, may recoil upon your own head.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Come on, Master Peter, let me know something.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: During the Sack of Rome, your son was captured by a certain Captain Orteca.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Are you sitting comfortably? Here comes the fairy tale.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: And because this captain was dividing his booty with two comrades, he tried to trick them out of their share of the spoils by sending us to Siena behind their backs. But after a few days, he became perturbed: he realized that Sienese gentlemen are lovers of justice and fair dealing, that they are friends to all citizens of Modena, and above all that they are men of honour. So he feared they might take Fabrizio from him, and liberate us. Therefore, he removed us from Siena, and sent us to a castle belonging to the Prince of Piombino; and from there he made us write off over and over again — per usque millies — for the thousand ducats which he had set as ransom.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Poor boy! At least they didn’t ill-treat him?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Not at all, he was treated according to his station.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: We never had any reply to the letters he made us write.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: There you are! He’s getting ready to touch you for the ransom now!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (ignoring Gherardo) Go on.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Well, after he had transferred us to the Spanish camp at Correggio, this captain was killed, and the court took possession of all his property and gave us our freedom.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: And where is my son?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Closer than you think.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: He’s not actually in Modena?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Master, if I may presume to expect the traditional reward for good news — quia omnis labor optat praemium — I shall tell you.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: So that’s your game, you charlatan!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: You are in the wrong, sir. I, a charlatan? Absit!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: You can have whatever you like. Where is he?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Here, at the inn, at the sign of the Fool’s Cap!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: That’s it. I can kiss good-bye to my thousand florins. But why should I care, as long as I get the girl? I’m rich enough already.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Come on, Master Peter, I can’t wait to see him, to hug him, to kiss him, and bounce him on my knee.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But master, he’s grown! Quanto mutatur ab illo! He’s not a little boy any more, to sit on your knee. You won’t recognize him, he’s so tall. And I don’t think he'll recognize you, you’ve changed so much. You’re wearing that beard now, which you didn’t have before, and I’d never have known you without hearing you speak. How is mistress Lelia?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Well, thank you. She’s filled out a bit too.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: What do you mean, ‘filled out’? If that’s the way things are, you can keep her — I’m not having her in that condition!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Calm down! All I meant was that she’s grown into a woman. Master Peter, I have not yet given you the embrace you deserve.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Master, I don’t want to boast unduly, but the things I've done for your son... well, you’d never imagine. And he’s deserved it all, he’s been as good as gold. Always amenable, always bending to my will.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Has he kept up with his studies?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: He’s never wasted time when circumstances permitted: per varios casus, per tot discrimina rerum ....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Call him out now, and don’t say anything. I want to see if he’ll know me.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: He went out of the inn a little while ago. Let’s see if he's come back yet.

div2.head: Scene 3

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (calls into the inn) Squint! Hey, Squint! Has Master Fabrizio come back?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Not yet.

div2.stage: (He emerges, drunker than ever; perhaps with Whisk supporting.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Come here, and say a few words to the old master. This is Master Virginio.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Have you cooled down yet?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Of course. You know I can’t stay angry with you for long.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Just as well.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Now give your hand to Fabrizio's father.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You give me your hand, then.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I don’t mean me. I mean this gentleman here.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Is this our young master’s father?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That’s right.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Most noble and generous master, you have arrived just in time to pay the bill. Welcome, sir.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: This man was a faithful servant to your son.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: What do you mean, ‘was’? I haven’t stopped being one, have I?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: God bless you, my fine lad! And be sure that those who have loyally kept him company will have their reward.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Boss, there’s only one thing I want in the whole world.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Ask, and it’s yours.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Buy me a place as apprentice with the landlord of this tavern here. He’s the best drinking companion a man ever had, and the best stocked and the wisest, and understands a traveller’s needs better than any landlord I’ve ever met. This is heaven on earth, boss, I don’t want to go anywhere else.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: He’s certainly got a reputation for his table.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Have you dined today?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Only a little.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: What have you had?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Oh, just a brace of partridges, half a dozen thrushes, a capon, a piece of veal, and I’ve only drunk two flagons.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Whisk, give him whatever he wants, and I’ll pay for it all.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Well, what do you want?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (Spanish accent, miming elaborate reverences) I kees your hhandos, señoros! That’s the kind of boss for me, professor! Master Peter, you’re a mean man, you always want to keep everything for yourself. You’ve been told over and over again. Whisk! Bring these gentlemen a little drink.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Not for me, thank you.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You’ll drink it when it comes. I’m paying. (Whisk comes out with drinks and snacks.) What do you think I am? Here, a few sweetbreads, a slice of sausage.... Go on, professor, drink up.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Very well then, if it means that we’ve made peace with each other.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: God, that’s good stuff! And boss, you must love and cherish this schoolteacher, whose eye your son is the apple of.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: God give him all prosperity.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You first, boss, and God afterwards. (To Gherardo) Another drink, your worship?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (his mind on other matters) Never mind about me.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Why don’t we all go inside, and wait for Fabrizio in the inn? And then, if supper’s ready, we could all have it here this evening.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Yes, perhaps that would be best.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I think I shall leave you — I have things to see to at home.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: (confidentially) You’ll make sure she doesn’t get away?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: That’s just what I had in mind.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: She’s all yours, do what you like with her. I give you a free hand.

div2.stage: (All except Gherardo go into the inn.)

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Well, I suppose one can’t expect to have everything. Never mind. But if my eyes aren’t playing me tricks, that’s Lelia herself, out in the street. That good-for-nothing maid must have let her get away.

div2.head: Scene 4
div2.stage: (Lelia and Clemenzia have come out of Clemenzia’s house.)

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: It’s no use, Clemenzia. Fortune is determined to play games with me, and then leave me with nothing.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: You set your heart at rest, and leave matters to me, and I’ll find some way of making you happy. Come in and get those clothes off: you mustn’t be seen like that any longer.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’m going to face her and find out how she escaped. Good day to you, Clemenzia; and to you, Lelia, my fair young bride. Who let you out of the house, then? That stupid Pasquella, I’ll be bound. I’m glad to see you came straight to your nurse, but to go on walking around in those clothes does no credit either to you or to me.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Oh heavens, he’s recognized me! Excuse me, sir, to who were you speaking? To Lelia? I’m not Lelia.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Come now! Just now, when your father and I shut you in with my daughter Isabella, didn’t you admit you were Lelia? And do you think now that I can’t recognize my own bride? Come along, let’s get rid of these clothes.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: The last thing I need now is a husband!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Go back home, Gherardo, my dear. All women do childish things of one sort or another. There’s not a single one of us who doesn’t kick over the traces once or twice. But it’s better to keep quiet about these things.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Nobody’s going to hear about it from me. But how did she get out of my house, when I’d locked her up with Isabella?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Who? Lelia?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: You’re making some mistake. She hasn’t been out of my sight all day. She just wanted to put on those clothes as a dressing-up game, as young girls will: she wanted to see if they suited her.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Don’t you try to pull the wool over my eyes. I tell you that we locked her indoors with Isabella.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Where have you come from now?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: From the Fool’s Cap tavern. I was there with Virginio.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Have you been drinking?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Only one small glass.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: I should go home and have a snooze. You sound as if you need it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let me just see Lelia properly for a moment before I go. I want to give her some good news.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: What news?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: That her brother has come back safe and sound, and that her father is waiting to see him at the inn.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: What? Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Fabrizio himself.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: If I thought that was true, I’d give you a kiss.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Delighted, I'm sure. I’d rather you gave me the chance to give one to Lelia.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: I must go and tell her straight away.

div2.stage: (She slips indoors and shuts Gherardo out.)

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: And I must go and tan the hide of that stupid hag who let her run away.

div2.stage: [But he gets distracted in some way, not explained by the authors, and goes off into town.]

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh good Lord almighty! I’ve had such a fright in there, I’ve had to come outside to get over it! And I’m sure that if I didn’t tell you ladies what it was, you’d never guess. I’ll tell you about it, on your own: I’m not going to tell those rotten men, they’d only split themselves laughing. Well: you know those two silly old suckers kept on saying that young man was a girl, and they shut him in the bedroom with my mistress Isabella, and gave me the key to look after. I decided to go in and see what they were up to, and I found them hugging and kissing each other like mad. I thought we’d better sort out once and for all whether he really was male or female, so my mistress held him down flat on the bed and got me to help her while she kept hold of his hands. He didn’t put up much of a struggle. So I undid him in front, and all of a sudden something goes ‘plonk’ into my hand. I didn’t stop to see whether it was a pestle or a carrot or a you know what, but whatever it was it certainly hadn’t been shrivelled by the frost. Well, my dears, the moment I saw it such a size — whoosh! — I was up and out and locked the door again. And I can tell you, I’m not going back in there alone: and if there’s anyone who doesn’t believe me, and wants to check, I’ll lend you the key. Oh Lord, there’s Lilias. Now I must see if I can trick him out of that necklace. These Spaniards reckon they’re so smart, they don’t think there’s anyone in the world who can get the better of them.

div2.head: Scene 6

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (to audience) Zere stands Pasquella. She avaits me viz impathienth, and ze time seems to hher mucho longo, so great is hher desire for my caresses. Ze cunning hhag knows already hhow expert is an Español in ze manipulathión of vomen. Hhow much bliss my compatriótës hhave brought to zese Italian hharlots!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (to audience) I’ve already worked out a way to leave him with the sticky end. Just you watch now.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (continues) Zis sordid vashervoman thinks zat I vill give hher ze rosary. But I shall make hher so milk hher old master, zat viz hhis money I buy doublets, hhoses and shirts, two at a time! Ze honor of ze Imperador is stakëd upon my sukthess! Now I vill take my pleasure viz hher, and zen take back my rosary and say nothing; for I think she no longer remembers.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (continues) If he once leaves that necklace in my hand, then he won’t set eyes on it ever again, if I can help it. And if he starts complaining, then I’ll get my old boy friend Pluck to give him the fright of his life.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (approaching her) Blessings upon ze muzzer hhoo bore you, and hhoo made you so hermosa, so courteous, so sinthere! I think you vere vaiting for me, no?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Ooooh, haven’t they got a way with words, these Spaniards! I’ve been waiting for you on this step for more than half an hour, just in case you passed by. My master was out, and we’d have been able to spend all that time together!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I regret so much my loss, por Diós , but I hhad many things to do. Now ve go in.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’m a bit afraid now that the master might come back. He’s been away quite a time. I bet you’ve forgotten that necklace, eh?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Not at all, my lady: it is hhere.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Show me. Hey, you were going to get that bead repaired! Why haven’t you done it?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I shall make it done anuzzer time. If I tell ze truth, I did not remember.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It shows how much you really care about me, doesn’t it, you heartless womaniser! It makes me want to....

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: No, no, liddle muzzer, do not be angry viz your son. You know, do you not, zat I am friend to no uzzer voman.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It doesn’t take long to catch you out, does it? Last time you said that you had two others, two ‘gentlewomen’ mooning over you.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I hhave abandonëd zem at vunce for you: I vant none uzzer zan yourselve. Do you not hhear?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: All right, I’ll believe you. Let’s see if this necklace really is a rosary. It looks rather long to me.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I do not know hhow many are ze beads.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: It shows how often you say your prayers. I bet you don't even know the words of the Paternoster. Give it here a minute and I’ll count them.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Take it zen — but let us go inside togezzer.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Here, take a look round, and make sure there’s no one watching you come inside.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (moves away to look) Hhere zere is nobody.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Right. (Looks inside the door of Gherardo’s house) Oh hell, all my chickens have got out. Stop there a moment, Lilias my love, in case they try to go that way. Otherwise it’ll take me all day to catch them again.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Be qvick, please.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Cheeeeeecky, chicky, chicky, chicky! Come along, my darlings! Chk, chk, chk! (etc.) I’ll wring your ruddy necks! I’m sure one’s going to get out. Be ready to stop it, Lilias.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat? Hhwere are zese chickens? I can see nothing, no cocks, no hhens.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Can’t you see them? Look, just here. Move a moment, let me shut the door until I’ve got them back in their coop.

div2.stage: (She slips indoors, with the rosary, and slams the door.)

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Oh! But you hhave bolted and chainëd ze door! Hhwy is zis?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: (inside) So the chickens won’t open it again.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Be qvick, zen. Someone might come and prevent our liddle business.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I don’t care who comes, sweetheart, because nobody is coming in here!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (catching on) You cursëd old hhore! Hhwy vill you not open?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You know what, my treasure? First of all, I think I’m going to recite the whole of this rosary. It’ll take all the evening, so you might as well push off for now. Oh yes, and I’ve just remembered another prayer, which I never miss saying on occasions like these.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat foolery is zis? Hhwat rosary? Hhwat prayer?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You want me to teach it to you? It’s a very potent incantation for getting rid of spooks. It always works. It goes like this:

lg.l: You came here with your tail up,
Birds of a feather flock together.
You tried to bring me stormy weather.
You thought that you could worse me,
But now you're left to curse me. Amen.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I do not understand zis prayer. If you vill not let me in, zen give me my rosary again and I vill go. By all ze hholy martyrs, zis lousy bawdy treacherous old hhag has dethievëd me! Madam Pasquella, open up! Qvickly, if you vish to live!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Poor me! Betrayed and abandoned yet again!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat? It is not true, lady Pasquella, hhe is hhere. Your boy is hhere, vaiting for you to open.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA

lg.l: (sings): ‘I’m sorry, my lord, I can’t oblige this evening.’

sp.p: Oh dear me!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Now ze bitch is making music as if I vere not hhere. I svear to God, I vill break ze door down!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Who’s there?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Your liddle son.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What do you want? I’m afraid the master’s out at the moment. Can I take a message?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: A vord viz you, please.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You could wait there, if you like. I’m sure he won’t be much longer.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Open, and I vill vait inside. She has gone avay. I svear by ze hhole vorld, zat if she does not give back my rosary, I vill burn ze hhouze down!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Hey! Who the hell’s that? That’s no way to behave! Who are you? Are you trying to smash the door down?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: By God and Saint Letania, I vill burn ze hhouze down, if you do not give me my rosary!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I think you must have got the wrong house. There are no rose trees in this garden.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: I am not saying zat: I am saying my Paternosters.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What’s it got to do with me if you’re saying your Paternosters? I learned mine a long time ago, I don’t need to practice alongside you.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: You filthy cowardly hhore! Do you take me for a lousy hheathen, converted only yesterday?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You know what? If you don’t clear off from in front of this door, you’ll get a bucketful of something on your head.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Throw your vater if you vill! It vill not suffice to qvench ze fire vhich I shall set to zis door! (Pasquella tips a bucket, or chamber-pot, over him from a window above.) Curse ze bitch! I am drenchëd, you lousy stinking old hhore! Hell and damnathión!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Did I wet you? Oh dear. But here comes the master. If there’s something you want, you can ask him about it, and stop messing me about.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: If zat old man finds me hhere, I shall be beaten blue and black. Better to retire from ze field.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: What are you hanging round the doorstep for, with that Spaniard? What business have you got with him?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: He was going on about a rose tree or something. I couldn’t make head or tale of it.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Now listen to me. Why can’t you do what you’re told once in a while? I’ve half a mind to give you what for.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What for?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Why did you let Lelia get out of the house? Didn’t I tell you not to open the door?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What do you mean? Isn’t she in the bedroom now?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: You know very well she isn’t.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: I’m quite sure she is.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: And I’m quite sure she’s not. I’ve just seen her over there in Clemenzia’s house.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: But I left the two of them in that room just now. On their knees, they were. Threading beads on their rosary.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Perhaps she got back ahead of me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: But I tell you she never got out. I can swear it. The room’s been locked the whole time.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Where’s the key?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Right here.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Give it to me. If she’s not there, I'm going to give you the hiding of your life.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: And if she is there, will you give me a new shift?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Right, it’s a bargain.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Let me open up, then.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (He goes in.) Oh no, I’m going to do that. You’d only pull some trick or other.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh Lord, I’m afraid he’s going to find them hard at it. But it’s some time since I left them — perhaps they’ve finished.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Pasquella, how long is it since my boy Fabio was here?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Because he’s betrayed me, and I’m going to punish him. And since Isabella has rejected me for him, she can expect the consequences too. It’s shameful, a gentlewoman of her rank falling for a page boy!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh don’t say things like that, sir. It’s only for your sake that she was kind to him.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: You can tell her from me that she’ll soon be sorry. As for him... you see this knife? The moment I lay hands on him, I’m going to cut off his lips and his ears, and tear his eyes out, and send the whole lot to Isabella on a platter. Then she can kiss them all to her heart’s content.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: That’s all bark and no bite. You won’t mend anything with that sort of talk.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: (He storms into his house.Gherardo come You wait and see!s running out from his own house.)

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Help! Treachery! I’ve been cheated, I’ve been swindled! That lying chiselling hypocrite Virginio, he’s made a fool of me! What am I going to do now?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What’s the matter, sir?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: What’s the matter? Who is that person in with my daughter?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: But you know, don’t you? It's Virginio’s little girl, isn’t it?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Little girl, eh? That ‘little girl’ will have my daughter producing little boys, damn and blast it!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Don’t use such language, sir! What’s the matter? Isn’t it Lelia?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: No it is not Lelia, it’s a man!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh what rubbish! What do you know about it?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I tell you I’ve seen with my own eyes!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: How do you mean?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Lying on top of my daughter, curse it!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: They were probably just having a little game.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I know what little game they were having.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Are you really sure it’s a man?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Only too sure. I opened the door on them without warning, and he’d got half his clothes off, and didn’t have time to cover up.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: But are you sure you really saw everything? It might have been a woman after all.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I tell you once and for all, he’s a man! There’s enough man there for two.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: What does Isabella say?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: What do you expect her to say? Oh the shame of it!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well why don’t you just let the young man go, and keep quiet? What are you going to do with him?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Do? I’m going to bring him up before the Governor General, and have him punished.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Perhaps he’ll run away.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’ve locked him in again. And here comes Virginio. Just the man I wanted to see.

div2.head: Scene 9
div2.stage: (Master Peter and Virginio come out of the inn.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I really don’t understand why he’s not back by now. I don’t know what to say.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Had he any weapon with him?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: He’s probably been picked up by the Watch. This new Prefect of Police we’ve got won’t let a flea slip through his net.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Surely they wouldn’t be so discourteous to a foreigner?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Good day to you, Virginio. Is this your notion of honourable behaviour? Is this how you treat your friends? A fine match you wanted to make between our two families! Who did you think you were cheating? Did you think I was just going to put up with it? You’d better watch out for yourself....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Have you got some grudge against me, Gherardo? What am I supposed to have done? It wasn’t me who wanted to make this match. You were pestering me about it for a whole year. If you’ve changed your mind now, we’ll simply call it off.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: And you’ve got the nerve to answer me back as though I were an idiot. Do you think I don’t know what’s going on? You cheating, swindling, lying crook! I’m going to take the whole matter before the Governor General.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Gherardo, insults like that are hardly suitable for a man of your standing — and particularly when they are addressed to me.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Do you think I’m going to stand here and not even complain, you scum? Do you suppose you can get away with anything, just because you’ve got your son back?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Scum yourself.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: My God, if I were a young man again, I’d chop you into little pieces!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Look, are you going to tell me what this is all about, or not?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: You shameless ruffian!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I’m not putting up with any more of this.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Thief!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Forger!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Liar! Just you wait....

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I’m waiting.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (trying to separate them) Come now, gentlemen! This is madness.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let go of me.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: And you, sir, put your coat back on.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Who does he think he’s dealing with? Send me back my daughter!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’ll skin you alive, and her too.

div2.stage: (He runs into his house to find something to do it with.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: What is this gentleman’s quarrel with you?

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I’ve no idea. Except that a little while ago I left my daughter Lelia in his house, because he was going to marry her. Now all of a sudden he’s making this fuss. I hope he doesn’t do her any harm.

div2.stage: (Gherardo rushes out of his house with a sharp implement and murderous intent. Virginio runs away.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: (intervening) Oh come now, please, good sir! That’s an offensive weapon, you know. Really, this is going too far.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let me get at him!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But what is the cause of your quarrel?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: That cheating swine has ruined me.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: I’ll chop him to bits. I’ll rip him apart with this cutter....

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But what has he done?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Let’s go indoors, since the lying bastard has run away, and I’ll tell you the whole thing. Aren’t you his son’s tutor, who was in the tavern with us just now?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: That is correct, sir.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Come inside.

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Can I rely on your good faith?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (They go into Gherardo’s house.) Of course.

div2.head: Scene 1
div2.stage: VIRGINIO; SQUINT; STOKE; GHERARDO; MASTER PETER; FABRIZIO
(Virginio, Stoke and Squint prepare to assault Gherardo’s house, with a motley array of weapons and armour.)

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Right, men, everybody follow me. That means you too, Squint.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: (still drunk) Are we supposed to be armed, or not? I haven’t got anything.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Go and borrow some equipment from the inn.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Boss, with a shield that size you ought to have a lance.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I can’t be bothered with a lance. This is good enough for me.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: Since you’re stripped down for duelling, perhaps you ought to have this buckler (i.e. his own rather inadequate means of defence). It would look much more dashing.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: No, this gives more protection. God, I can’t wait to get at that thieving ruffian! Goodness knows what he’s done to that poor girl. He might even have killed her.

div2.stage: (Squint staggers out with a kitchen spit, the meat still on it, and probably some pots and pans as armour.)

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: This’ll do for me, boss. I’ll skewer him on this spit like a plucked woodcock.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: What do you need the meat for?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: We old campaigners know that the first thing an army needs is provisions.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: And what’s that bottle for?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: To refresh and sustain the troops, if their first assault is beaten off.

sp.speaker: STOKE
sp.p: That’s just as well, ’cause it will be.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Right! Let me get at ’em. I’ll have the old man and his daughter and all the household skewered side by side like a row of little kidneys over a stove. I’ll spit the old man in through his arse and out through his eyes, and all the others sideways like little roasting thrushes.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: The door seems to be open. Do you think they’ve prepared an ambush?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: An ambush? I don’t fancy that. If they’re in hiding, they might give us a hiding. Hey, there’s the Professor!

div2.stage: (Master Peter comes out of Gherardo’s house.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Don’t worry, Gherardo, sir! Leave it all to me, and I promise to set everything to rights.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: You be careful, boss! That ruddy schoolteacher’s probably deserted to the enemy. His sort always do that: they can never stand firm in a tight spot. Shall I skewer him now, and it’ll be first blood to us? us? [Production experience suggests that this is a good moment for a scene of fairly extensive slapstick violence and mayhem, involving as many characters as possible.]

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: But Virginio sir, master, why all these weapons?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: There you are. I told you.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: What’s happened to my daughter? Give her to me now so I can take her home. And have you found Fabrizio?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Yes sir, I have.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Where is he?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: He’s in here, and he’s found himself a fine wife, if you’re prepared to give your consent.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: A wife? Who?

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: That’s quick work. We’re rich, we’re rich!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: A beautiful and well-bred young lady — Gherardo’s daughter.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: But Gherardo was trying to murder me just now!

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Rem omnem a principio audies : you shall hear the whole thing from the beginning. If you would like to come inside, we can tell you all about it. Would you come out now, Gherardo sir?

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: (coming out) Oh Virginio, you’ll never believe what’s happened! The most amazing chance! Come along in.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Shall I spit him now, boss? But he’s too tough to be worth cooking.

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Put all those weapons away, it’s a lot of nonsense.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Can I trust you?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: I can answer for your safety, sir.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: Well then. You others go back home, get rid of your weapons, and bring me back my robe.

div2.stage: (Exit Squint and Stoke. Master Peter brings out Fabrizio.)

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: Fabrizio, come and be re-united with your father.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: But isn’t this Lelia?

sp.speaker: MASTER PETER
sp.p: No, this is Fabrizio.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: My son!

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: I’ve waited so long for this!

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: My son, I thought you were lost for ever!

sp.speaker: GHERARDO
sp.p: Inside, everyone, and hear the whole story. And if you’re worried about your daughter, she’s safe at home with Clemenzia.

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: God be praised!

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: But he’s in Clemenzia’s house, I tell you. I’ve seen him there, and heard him.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Are you sure it was Fabio?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Do you think I don’t know him?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Let’s go there, then. And if I get my hands on him....

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Calm down, you’ll ruin everything. Control yourself until you can get him out of there.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How am I supposed to control myself?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: If you don’t, you’ll spoil the whole plan.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Let it spoil.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: (inside) Who’s there?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: A friend. Come down a moment, Clemenzia.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Oh! Master Flamminio. What do you want, sir?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Open up, and I’ll tell you.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: I’ll be down in a moment.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: As soon as she opens the door, push your way in, see if he’s there, and call me.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Leave it to me.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: (opening the door) What can I do for you, sir?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What are you doing with my page boy in your house?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: What page boy? And where do you think you’re going, pusher? (She succeeds in keeping Sifter out.) Are you trying to force an entry to my house?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Clemenzia, I swear by the holy immaculate... if you don’t give me back...

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Give you back what?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: My page boy who’s hiding in your house.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: There are no page boys of yours in my house, though you might find a chamber maid if you looked.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Clemenzia, this is no time for foolery. We’ve always been friends, you and I: you’ve done favours for me, and I’ve done some for you. This time it’s something really important.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: In other words, something to do with a woman, by the looks of it. Now just you give yourself time to cool down a little.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I’m asking you to give me Fabio.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: So I shall.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Right. Get him down, then.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Take it a little easy, for goodness’ sake! You young men are always so hasty, you’re no use to a woman at all. How are things with Isabella?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I’d like to rip her apart!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Go on! You can’t mean it.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Can’t I? She’s made it pretty clear what she means.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, whatever she’s done, it serves you right. There’s no gratitude in you young men, you can never recognize your obligations

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: That is not true of me. I know well that I have my faults, but ingratitude is not one of them. It’s a thing I detest, I’m the last man in the world to be charged with that.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, perhaps not you, then. But there is another young gentleman in Modena, rather like yourself, who started taking an interest in a girl here; and she fell for him in return, so desperately that she had eyes for no one else in the world.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: He’s a lucky man, then. I wish I could say the same in my case.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, it happened that the girl’s father sent her away from Modena for a while. And when she left, she was in such tears as you’ve never seen, for fear he should forget her while she was gone. And in fact he turned straight away to another woman, as though the first had never existed for him.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Then that man is not a gentleman, as you said he was. He is an ungrateful deserter.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: But there is worse to come. When the young girl came back a few months later, and found her lover was in love with a woman who cared nothing for him, then to do him service she left her house and her father, and put her honour at risk. She dressed as a page boy, and got herself hired as a servant by the man she loved.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: This actually happened in Modena?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: And you know both the young people concerned.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I would rather be loved as that man was loved than be Duke of Milan.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: And then what happens? This lover of hers still didn’t know her, and he used her as go-between to carry messages to that other woman; and that poor girl, just to give him pleasure, did exactly as she was told.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Now that is true virtue, true loyalty! An example for all time! Why could such a thing not happen to me?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well... in any case, even if it did, you’d never give up Isabella.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I'd give up... I nearly said Christ, for a woman like that. Please, Clemenzia, can’t you tell me who she is?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, I could. But first of all, I want you to tell me, on your honour as a knight and a gentleman, what you would do to that poor young woman if such a thing happened to you. Would you throw her out, when you heard what she’d done? Would you kill her? Or would you think that she deserved some recompense?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I swear to you by the sun you see in the sky: may I never be seen again in honourable society if I would not prefer that woman as my wife before the Duke of Ferrara’s daughter — even if she were ugly, even if she were poor, even if she were of low birth.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: You’re saying a great deal. Do you swear it?

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: I swear it, and I would do it.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: (to Sifter) You’re witness to that.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I heard. And I know he’d do it, too.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Now I shall tell you the names of that girl and that young gentleman. Fabio! Fabio! Come down here, your master wants you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What shall I do, Sifter? Should I kill this traitor or not? He’s always been a very able servant.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: I wondered how long you’d keep it up. I knew it all along. Go on, forgive him, what else? In any case, that giddy Isabella never cared anything about you.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: That’s very true.

div2.head: Scene 3
div2.stage: CLEMENZIA; FLAMMINIO; SIFTER; LELIA in woman’s clothes; PASQUELLA
(Clemenzia brings Lelia out. Pasquella comes out of Gherardo’s house.)

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Yes, all right, leave it to me. I’ll tell her everything you’ve said. I’m not daft.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, master Flamminio, this is your servant Fabio. Take a good look. Do you know him? You look a little surprised. But this is that very same faithful, loving girl whom I was telling you about. Look at her, see if you recognize her. Have you lost your tongue? Why is that? You yourself are that young man, with so little appreciation of his lady’s love. This is the truth, now — no more deceptions. You know if I’m telling the truth or not. Now it’s for you to attend to what you swore to do, or I’ll call you out in public for breach of promise.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: If this is a deception, then I can’t think of a better way to be deceived. How could I be so blind that I didn’t know her?

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: What about me then, after all those times when I wanted to see for myself? I’ve been a complete ruddy idiot.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Clemenzia! Virginio says you’ve got to come to our house straight away, because his son Fabrizio who came home today is getting married, and you’ve got to go home to tidy up, because you know there are no other women there to see to things.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Getting married? Who to?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: To Isabella, my master Gherardo’s daughter.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: What? Do you mean your Isabella, Gherardo Foiani’s daughter, or some other?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Some other who? No, I mean her. He knows what he’s about, that young man — he went straight to the honey pot.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Are you sure?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Absolutely. I saw the whole thing: they exchanged rings, hugs and kisses, and everyone was delighted. And before he gave her the ring, my mistress had already given him... well, never mind.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: How long ago was all this?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Right now, this very minute. And they sent me straight off at the double to tell Clemenzia and fetch her over.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well, you tell them that I’ll only be a little moment. Go along.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: I can’t believe it — my brother! So many wonderful things, all at once!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Don't be long, then, because I’ve got so much to do myself that I don’t know which end is which. First of all I’ve got to go and buy some make-up for her. Oh yes, I forgot to ask if you’ve got Lelia at home with you — because Gherardo has accepted her again.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: You can see for yourself that she’s here. But does he really mean to marry her off to your spineless bogey of a master? He ought to be ashamed of himself.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You don’t know my master. If you knew how lively he can be, you wouldn’t say that.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Well you ought to know. You’ve probably tried him out.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Same as you have with yours. I’m off now.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: They can’t want to marry her to Gherardo?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: They do, worse luck. Poor child, nothing seems to go right for her.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: He can go and croak first, if I have anything to do with it. Listen, Clemenzia, I’m sure this has all come about by the will of God, who has taken pity on this loyal young girl and given me a chance to save my soul and make restitution. So, my lady Lelia, if you are willing, I hereby take you as my promised wife. And I swear on my honour as a knight and a gentleman that if I cannot have you, I shall have no other woman.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Flamminio, you are my lord, and you know well what I did and why I did it. I have no other desire in the world.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: As you have truly shown. And forgive me if I have done anything to hurt you during the time when I did not know you, for I recognize my error and am greatly ashamed.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: My lord Flamminio, nothing that you could do can give me anything but pleasure.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Clemenzia, I do not want to delay matters and allow time for anything to interfere with our good fortune. I should like to marry her now, if she is willing.

sp.speaker: LELIA
sp.p: Very willing.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Thanks be to God! And you, master, my lord Flamminio, are you willing? Be it known that I hereby appoint myself notary at law — and these are my qualifications.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: More willing to do this than anything I have ever done.

sp.speaker: SIFTER
sp.p: Very good. You may now marry, and proceed to bed in your own time. Hey, I didn’t say you could kiss her!

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: Do you know what I think now? You two should go into my house, while I tell Virginio what’s happened, and see Gherardo’s face when he hears the news.

sp.speaker: FLAMMINIO
sp.p: Yes please, and tell Isabella too.

div2.stage: (Flamminio, Lelia and Sifter go into Clemenzia’s house. Clemenzia to Gherardo’s house.)

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Por la vida del rey! Hhoo do I see but zat sneaking bitch Pasquella, hhoo mockëd me and robbëd me of my beads by dethepthión. Hhwat luck to find hher again!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Oh hell, here comes the old nag-bag himself! He would have to turn up now. I wish he’d go and boil his head, and the rest of his regiment along with him. How am I going to get out of this one?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Madam Pasquella!

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: That’s a good start. I’m a madam already.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Madam, you hhave mockëd me, and you hhave taken my rosary, and you hhave not done zose things vhich you promisëd you vould do....

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Sssshh! Keep your voice down, for God’s sake!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat for? Zere is no vun hhere hhoo can hhear us.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Are you trying to ruin me?

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Are you trying to dethieve me?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Push off now, and leave me alone. I’ll talk to you another time.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Return to me my rosary, and zen say vhat you vant. I vill not let you able to say zat you dethievëd me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: You can have it back another time. Do you think I’m carrying it around with me? It’s not all that precious, you know: there are plenty of other people who’ll give me necklaces.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwy did you enclose me out of your door, and zen make musics and songs, and zen said something ‘Bogeyman, bogeyman’, and prayers and uzzer nonsensicals?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Keep it quiet! You’re ruining me. I’ll tell you the whole thing.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Hhwat hhole thing? Go on, zen.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Come over into this corner, so the mistress won’t see us.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Is zis anuzzer trick or no?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Me trick you? Am I the sort of person that goes around playing tricks on people? Come now.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Now tell me — hhwat is all zis?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Well. You remember we were talking together. Well. My mistress Isabella had sneaked down the stairs, and was hiding right next to me and listening to every word we said. When I was chasing the chickens, she slipped into the bedroom and was watching what we were up to through a crack in the door. But I spotted her, and pretended I hadn’t, so I had to make out I’d been trying to trick you, and I showed her the rosary afterwards to prove it. She took it, because she thought I’d done you out of it, and she’s wearing it now as a bracelet. But I’ll get it back off her tonight, and give it back to you, if you’ve decided not to give it to me after all.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Can zis be ze truth? Bevare zat you do not dethieve me.

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: My dear Lilias, if it’s not the absolute truth may I never set eyes on you again! Do you think I’m not proud of your friendship? You’re so suspicious, you Spaniards. It’s a wonder you believe in Jesus Christ, since you don’t seem to believe anything else you’re told.

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: Vell now, hhwy do ve not do hhwat ve had agreed betveen ourselves?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: My mistress has just got engaged, and the wedding’s this evening, so I’ve got much too much work to do. We’ll have to wait for another time. (To herself) Ugh, they really turn your stomach, this lot!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (from a distance) Mañana , zen, tomorrow? Tomorrow morning, yes? Is it not so?

sp.speaker: PASQUELLA
sp.p: Leave it to me. I’ll remember you when the time comes. Don’t worry. Whew! Crikey!

sp.speaker: LILIAS
sp.p: (calls after her) I svear to God, if you dethieve me vun more time, I shall slap you on ze face!

div2.head: Scene 5
div2.stage: (Listening intently at a window of her own house)

sp.speaker: THE GIRL
sp.p: Hey, there’s an awful lot of thrashing about in this downstairs room. I wonder what it is. There’s a bed in there, heaving and shaking about as if it were haunted. Oooooh, I’m frightened! What’s that? There’s someone in there moaning, and saying ‘Ooh, not so hard!’ And there’s someone else, what’s he saying? ‘My darling, my love, my angel, my wife!’ (Giggles.) I can’t hear the rest. Do you think I should knock and ask them to speak up? Oh! One’s saying ‘Wait for me’. They must be going somewhere. And there’s the other saying ‘Be quick then!’ Are they trying to smash that bed? It’s going faster and faster.... Help! I’m going to tell my mum!

div2.head: Scene 6

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: I was convinced you were somebody I knew, a gentleman’s servant in this town, who looks so much like you that he must be your brother.

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Other people have been mistaking me today. I was beginning to think that the landlord had swapped me for someone else while I was sleeping at the inn.

sp.speaker: ISABELLA
sp.p: Here’s your nurse Clemenzia, come to have a word.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: (following them out of the house) This must be him. He’s the very image of Lelia. Fabrizio, my darling boy, welcome home. How are you?

sp.speaker: FABRIZIO
sp.p: Dear old nurse! I’m very well. How’s Lelia?

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: She’s doing very well too. But let’s go in, there’s so much for us all to talk about.

div2.stage: (She waves Fabrizio and Isabella into her own house, but is held back by Virginio’s approach)

sp.speaker: VIRGINIO
sp.p: I’m so pleased to have found my son that I’ll agree to whatever you like.

sp.speaker: CLEMENZIA
sp.p: It's God’s will, sir, believe me. So much better than marrying her off to an old man with no backbone like Gherardo. Let me go in now and check how things are, because I left the young couple very intent on each other, and they’re all by themselves. Come in now, sir. Everything is all right.

sp.speaker: SQUINT
sp.p: Evening, your worships. Don’t expect any of that lot to come outside again: the play’s been long enough already. If you want to join us at the wedding supper, then I’ll see you all at the Fool’s Cap. But bring some cash with you, because you’ll have to pay for yourselves. But if you aren’t coming — and you don’t look as if you are — then stay here and have a good time. Members of the Academy: your appreciation, please!
